He was looking down, and now he looked up at her, his forehead crinkling for an instant. He let go. “What should I call you?”
The question startled her; she had to think for a moment before she answered. “Mara,” she said again, trying to decide whether that was what she meant, or just what sounded good for some reason.
“Okay.” His smile broadened, but he didn’t say anything else. He stood there with his hands in his pockets, waiting for her to speak. She wanted to ask how the two of them had gotten the same name—how often did that happen?—but she didn’t dare do so yet. Instead she glanced around the room, looking for something else to comment on. There were couches and tables, chairs and a bookshelf and a big-screen TV in the corner. “Is this where you guys meet?” she asked, gesturing at the furnishings.
“Yes.”
“And are all these things here because that’s what people like?”
“No, not really. More like—” He gestured at one of the couches. “—this one was free.”
text:
When Mara walked into the common room at six fifteen, someone was already there. Someone younger, it seemed.
She couldn’t make out the face behind the blond hair. But the body was fine enough, leaning back on the couch with bare legs crossed and arms flung in opposite directions, one palm pressing the padded wall and the other wrist resting on the low table beside him.
She stood stock-still by the doorway for a moment, aware of her breath and of his awareness that she was here. He stirred and tilted his head; a face turned toward her, expressionless.

The two pairs of eyes held each other through an entire exhale.
And then the young man had pushed himself up on the armrests, stretched to his full height, and strolled over to shake her hand.
“Mara?”
He was closer than she would have guessed from where he’d been sitting, broad-shouldered and strong-chinned in a white T-shirt, grinning at her through dark-framed glasses as he reached out for the handshake. She took it.
“Jonah,” he said.
“Hello,” she replied, and then they stood there, still shaking hands, not knowing what to do next.

He was looking down, and now he looked up at her, his forehead crinkling for an instant. He let go. “What should I call you?”
The question startled her; she had to think for a moment before she answered. “Mara,” she said again, trying to decide whether that was what she meant, or just what sounded good for some reason.
“Okay.” His smile broadened, but he didn’t say anything else. He stood there with his hands in his pockets, waiting for her to speak. She wanted to ask how the two of them had gotten the same name—how often did that happen?—but she didn’t dare do so yet. Instead she glanced around the room, looking for something else to comment on. There were couches and tables, chairs and a bookshelf and a big-screen TV in the corner. “Is this where you guys meet?” she asked, gesturing at the furnishings.
“Yes.”
“And are all these things here because that’s what people like?”
“No, not really. More like—” He gestured at one of the couches. “—this one was free.”

segment:
The room was quieter than when she’d been here before; fewer voices were coming from other directions. Some of the chairs had been rearranged, and two of them now sat empty at the far side. Mara took a few steps toward them—

And that was the moment when the young man's eyes widened and he broke out into a smile.
Mara wasn’t sure if she’d ever seen his teeth before or not, but now they looked remarkably white against his pink lips. She couldn’t help returning the grin as well.

“Jonah?” Mara asked, her voice trailing off to a question mark because this seemed very strange and also somehow appropriate? Was it just that he wasn't what she'd been expecting? “You... you live here, then?”

Jonah nodded enthusiastically, letting go of her hand finally as he pulled open the door to the main hallway outside.
“I do,” he said brightly, stepping back from the entranceway so that Mara would have plenty of room to follow him through. “Do you mind if we go into my office?”
Mara blinked.
“Your office?”
